nodes.title: The lesson A/B has 36 independent comparisons, not 60 -- 1.67 lessons ride on each one -- and only 3 of those 36 rounds could have shown a difference at all: treated won 2, control won 1, exact p = 0.25
nodes.body:
gap-w1-004 (and ctx-033, the same question asked by a different wave) says the knowledge arm's value is unevidenced. exp-lesson-001 answered that we run the experiment: 60 `lesson.impact` rows, mean delta +0.017. e69 measures what those rows can support, and the first finding is that the row is not the observation.

**The unit is the round.** `lesson.impact` is emitted **per injected lesson**, so 60 rows cover only **36 distinct rounds** -- 1.67 lessons per comparison. Every lesson injected into the same round rides on the same treated-vs-control comparison, so their deltas are copies of one number. Counting 60 inflates n by 1.67x and, worse, pretends that 25 lessons got 60 independent tests when 11 rounds tested two or three lessons at once. Collapsing to rounds: 36 observations.

**The arm flips, and the sign convention holds.** The treated arm is a2 in 48 rows and a1 in 12, so a comparison that assumed "treated = second candidate" would be measuring candidate index in a fifth of the data. Pinning the arm from the event's own `attempt`/`control` fields and recomputing treated-minus-control reproduced the recorded delta in **36 of 36 rounds, 0 violations** -- so the ledger's arithmetic is right and the only defect was how I was about to aggregate it.

**Three of 36 rounds could move.** 33 of 36 rounds passed in both arms, which is the structural zero: the task's bar was already met, both candidates cleared it, and no lesson could have produced a delta. 0 rounds failed in both arms. **3 rounds disagreed**, and on those the treated arm won **2** and the control **1**. Exact two-sided sign test on 3 discordant pairs: **p = 0.25**. A +1/36 = +2.8pp point estimate with a 95% interval that spans zero by a wide margin.

**What the design could have detected.** With a disagreement rate of 0.083, the standard error of the paired mean at n=36 is **0.048**, so the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is **13.5 percentage points**. The literature effect sizes worth caring about are +5.5 to +9.9pp (ctx-033), i.e. below the floor. Reaching a 5pp effect at this disagreement rate needs **262 rounds**; at the observed median round of 390 s that is **28 hours of continuous rounds** for one experiment, and 0.10 needs 66 rounds (~7 hours).

So the honest answer to 'is the knowledge arm worth its extra call' is not 'null': it is **underpowered by a factor of ~7 against the smallest effect anyone has published, with 92% of its rounds structurally unable to produce a signal.** The 3 discordant rounds are not noise on a flat surface -- they are the same narrow band exp-slot-004 found (a1 passes, a2 fails, in the rounds where the task is genuinely on the edge), which is exactly where a tie-break decides and therefore the only place a lesson could ever show up.
nodes.source: research/exp/e69.mjs over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns/*/events.jsonl (60 lesson.impact rows, 25 lessons, 36 rounds); event written by src/runtime/round.js lesson.impact block

nodes.title: A per-item event logged for a per-batch comparison double-counts the experiment: the row count is not n, and 92% of the rounds could not have produced a signal whatever the treatment did
nodes.body:
The ledger was not lying. `lesson.impact` genuinely records one row per lesson, and the mean of those rows is genuinely +0.017. The error is in the reader: taking the row as the unit of observation when the comparison happens once per round. Both facts are visible in the same file -- 60 rows, 36 rounds -- and nothing in the row says 'I am a copy'. Any event emitted inside a loop over a collection will have this property, and the tell is a non-integer ratio of rows to the thing being tested (here 1.67 lessons/round).

The second finding is stronger than the underpowering, and it is not about statistics. **33 of 36 rounds passed in both arms.** That is not a null result; it is a ceiling. The treated and control arms were both handed a task that two independent candidates could solve, so the experiment was mostly run on ground where no treatment could show an effect -- the same mechanism that makes the campaign-level pass rate saturate in round 1 (56 of 67 campaigns) and that `exp-gate-004` found makes each task's promotion a one-shot event. A trial whose sample is 92% at ceiling reports the ceiling, not the treatment.

Put together: the honest summary of the knowledge arm after two years of rounds is *not measured*, and it is not measured for a reason that is fixable in one place -- the arm must be run on rounds where the task is not already solved, which is the same set of rounds where the loop has something to learn. That is a scheduling decision, not a bigger sample: 262 rounds of ceiling would cost 28 hours and still return p > 0.05.

Limits. The 3 discordant rounds are all in the same handful of campaigns (loom-acc2, loom-self2, loom-self3) and each is one task (planning-chip, plateau, policydiff), so even the +2.8pp point estimate is really three coin flips. And this whole analysis is about the ledger's own A/B, which uses the loop's binary score; a graded metric (exp-diff-006 proved the machinery works end to end) would give each round a continuous outcome and change the power arithmetic completely -- 36 rounds of graded delta is a much better experiment than 36 rounds of a coin.
nodes.source: research/exp/e69.mjs; cross-reference exp-slot-004/005 (the disagreement band), exp-gate-004 (one-shot promotion), exp-diff-006 (graded end-to-end)

gaps.title: Can the treated/control arm be restricted to rounds where the task is unsolved, and does that need a scheduler change or only a flag?
gaps.body: exp-lesson-002 found 33 of 36 lesson A/B rounds passed in both arms, so 92% of the experiment was run at ceiling. Restricting the arm to rounds with headroom would multiply the information per round by roughly 12x, which turns the 262-round requirement for a 5pp effect into ~22 rounds -- about 2.4 hours instead of 28. The mechanism to do it exists: `exp-lesson-001` notes the treated arm is assigned by candidate index, and the selector already prefers unsolved tasks (`pickTask` in src/runtime/selector.js), so the two policies are fighting: the selector chooses an unsolved task, but by the time both candidates are scored the task may already be solved by the first one. What is not known is whether restricting to headroom is even legal for the loop's own purposes -- a lesson injected on an already-solved task is wasted research, but skipping the arm changes what a promotion means. Recording the arm's task-headroom state at assignment time would let a replay answer this from existing rounds instead of running new ones.
